authors: Zhihong Shao*, Peiyi Wang*, Qihao Zhu*, Runxin Xu, Junxiao Song, Xiao Bi, Haowei Zhang, Mingchuan Zhang, Y.K. Li, Y. Wu, Daya Guo* (* core contributors; Shao, Wang and Zhu as interns at DeepSeek-AI)

code.title: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-Math
code.note: the official repository: MIT-licensed code (inference and evaluation scripts), the three 7B checkpoints under the DeepSeek Model License (commercial use permitted); no training code, no RL code and no corpus. About 20 minutes for the README and the evaluation entry point

takeaway: GRPO replaces PPO's critic with a group-mean reward baseline (advantage = z-scored reward across G samples per question, KL moved into the loss), taking a 7B math model to 51.7% MATH and becoming the default RLVR algorithm.
verdict: Believe the data pipeline and the headline scores: the gains are large against the noise. Treat GRPO's superiority as an argument, not a result: the paper never trains PPO, its memory saving is asserted rather than measured, and GRPO's lead over Online RFT in its own ablation is within one standard error. GRPO's standing rests on cost and on what later work found.

headline.k: DeepSeekMath-RL 7B, top-1, chain-of-thought, no tools: the first open model over 50% without tools
headline.d: +4.9 points over the Instruct model (46.8%), about 5 standard errors on 5,000 problems

headline.k: the DeepSeekMath Corpus: 35.5M math pages mined from Common Crawl in four fastText rounds
headline.d: 8.8 times OpenWebMath, 6.9 times Minerva's math web pages

headline.k: GRPO is never trained against PPO here; the saving is argued from the diagram (Figure 4), not measured
headline.d: the first published head-to-head came with DeepSeek-R1, a year later
